style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare-transliteration in amp with Strong's carried in notes (matching the ch.1 pilot); em-dashes used sparingly.
chapterNote: Chapter 24 closes the long collection of the wise with a string of warnings and pictures, then appends a coda of 'further sayings of the wise' (vv. 23-34). The opening movement returns to a theme that haunts the book: do not envy the wicked or crave their company (vv. 1-2, 19-20), for their house is built on violence while the righteous house is built by wisdom, understanding, and knowledge (vv. 3-6). Between these bookends stand sharp single proverbs -- on courage in adversity (v. 10), on rescuing those dragged toward death (vv. 11-12), on the resilience of the righteous who fall seven times and rise (v. 16), and on refusing to gloat over a fallen enemy (vv. 17-18). The coda warns judges against partiality (vv. 23-25), commends the honest answer (v. 26), counsels working the field before building the house (v. 27), and ends with the unforgettable parable of the sluggard's overgrown vineyard (vv. 30-34) -- a field the writer walks past, considers, and turns into a lesson.

1.text: Do not burn with envy toward evil men, nor crave their company,
1.amp: Do not be envious [qana -- to be jealous, to be consumed with zealous longing] toward evil [ra] men, neither desire [avah -- to crave, to long for] to be with them,
1.notes: qana (H7065) is the heated word for jealousy or zeal -- here a covetous longing for what the wicked have. The same warning frames this movement and returns at v.19. avah (H183) is intense craving; the temptation is not just to copy the wicked but to want a seat among them.

2.text: for their heart plots violence, and their lips speak nothing but trouble.
2.amp: for their heart [leb] broods [hagah -- to mutter, to mull, to devise] on destruction [shod -- ruin, violent plunder], and their lips [saphah] speak [dabar] of trouble [amal -- toil, misery, harm].
2.notes: hagah (H1897) is the low muttering of meditation -- the wicked rehearse violence the way the righteous rehearse God's law (cf. Ps 1:2). What they store in the heart, the lips inevitably spill; amal (H5999) is the wearying mischief their words breed.

3.text: By wisdom a house is built, and by understanding it is set on a firm foundation;
3.amp: Through wisdom [chokmah -- skill in living] a house [bayith] is built [banah], and by understanding [tebunah -- discernment] it is established [kun -- made firm, set steady],
3.notes: chokmah (H2451) and tebunah (H8394) are paired as the architect's tools: wisdom raises the walls, understanding sets them on a foundation that holds. kun (H3559) means to be firmly fixed -- the opposite of the wicked house built on the shifting sand of violence (v.2).

4.text: and by knowledge its inner rooms are filled with every precious and pleasant treasure.
4.amp: and by knowledge [daat] the chambers [cheder -- the inner rooms, the private spaces] are filled [male] with all precious [yaqar -- rare, costly] and pleasant [naim -- lovely, delightful] riches [hon -- wealth, substance].
4.notes: the trio completes the building of v.3: chokmah, tebunah, daat (H1847) furnish what they construct. The cheder (H2315) is the innermost room, the place a household keeps its dearest things -- true wealth is not flaunted in the street but stored in the heart of a wisely built home.

5.text: A wise man is mighty in strength, and a man of knowledge makes his power greater still.
5.amp: A wise [chakam] man is in strength [oz -- might, force], and a man [ish] of knowledge [daat] strengthens [amats -- braces, makes firm] his power [koach -- ability, vigor].
5.notes: the Hebrew literally reads 'a wise man is in strength' -- wisdom is itself a kind of might. amats (H553) is to fortify or make resolute; knowledge does not replace strength but multiplies it, so that the wise outmatch the merely strong (cf. v.6; Eccl 9:16).

6.text: For by wise strategy you wage your war, and victory is found in a multitude of counselors.
6.amp: For by wise counsel [tachbulot -- steering strategies, sound guidance] you shall make [asah] your war [milchamah], and in the multitude [rob -- abundance] of counselors [yoets -- those who advise and plan] there is safety [teshuah -- deliverance, victory].
6.notes: tachbulot (H8458) comes from a root for ropes -- the steering lines of a ship, the 'strategies' that pilot a campaign (cf. 1:5, 11:14). teshuah (H8668) is deliverance or victory; the wise win not by lone heroics but by listening widely before they strike.

7.text: Wisdom is too lofty for a fool; in the gate, where matters are decided, he has nothing to say.
7.amp: Wisdom [chokmot -- wisdom in her fullness] is too high [rum -- exalted, out of reach] for a fool [evil]; he does not open [pathach] his mouth [peh] in the gate [shaar -- the city gate, the seat of judgment].
7.notes: chokmot (H2454) is the plural-intensive form, wisdom personified in her heights -- coral hung above the fool's reach (cf. Job 28:18). The shaar (H8179), the city gate, was the courtroom and council of the town; the fool, having nothing wise to offer there, stays silent among the elders.

8.text: Whoever schemes to do harm will be known to all as a master of mischief.
8.amp: He who devises [chashab -- to plot, to reckon, to plan] to do evil [raa -- to act wickedly] shall be called [qara -- named, proclaimed] a master [baal -- owner, lord] of schemes [mezimmah -- intrigue, calculated plots].
8.notes: chashab (H2803) is the planning mind turned to evil; the schemer earns a title that sticks -- baal (H1167) mezimmah (H4209), 'lord of plots.' Reputation follows pattern: a man becomes publicly known by what he privately devises.

9.text: The scheming of folly is sin itself, and the mocker is detestable to everyone.
9.amp: The scheme [zimmah -- a wicked plan, devising] of foolishness [ivvelet -- folly] is sin [chattath]; and the scorner [luts -- the mocker, the one who sneers] is an abomination [toevah -- a detestable thing] to men [adam].
9.notes: zimmah (H2154) names the very plotting of v.8 as chattath (H2403), sin -- the plan is guilty before the deed is done. The luts (H3887), the habitual mocker, is toevah (H8441): not merely disliked but loathed, the same strong word reserved elsewhere for what God Himself detests.

10.text: If you go slack in the day of distress, how small your strength has proved to be.
10.amp: If you faint [raphah -- to grow slack, to let the hands drop] in the day [yom] of adversity [tsarah -- distress, the narrow pressing place], your strength [koach] is small [tsar -- narrow, cramped].
10.notes: the verse turns on a sound-play the kit preserves: tsarah (H6869), the day of trouble, and tsar (H6862), narrow -- adversity is the 'narrow place,' and the man who slackens (raphah, H7503) there discovers his own strength was just as narrow. Crisis does not weaken the man; it reveals what strength was really there.

11.text: Rescue those being dragged off to death, and hold back those staggering toward slaughter.
11.amp: Deliver [natsal -- snatch away, rescue] those who are taken [laqach] to death [mavet], and those who totter [mot -- stagger, slip] toward the slaughter [hereg -- killing], hold them back.
11.notes: natsal (H5337) is the rescue verb -- to seize a man back from the brink. The picture is of prisoners led to execution; the wise are not allowed the luxury of looking away. Indifference to a neighbor's mortal danger is itself a sin (cf. v.12).

12.text: If you protest, 'But we knew nothing of this,' does not He who weighs the heart discern it? Does not the Keeper of your soul know? And will He not repay each man according to what he has done?
12.amp: If you say [amar], 'Behold, we did not know [yada] it,' does not He who weighs [takan -- measures, tests the balance of] the heart [leb] discern [biyn] it? And He who keeps [natsar -- guards, watches over] your soul [nephesh], does He not know? And will He not render [shub -- return, repay] to each man [adam] according to his deed [poal]?
12.notes: the excuse of ignorance is dismantled by three divine attributes: God weighs the heart (takan, H8505, the same verb for measuring out the heavens, Isa 40:12), He guards the soul (natsar, H5341), and He repays the deed (shub, H7725, here 'render back'). The God who searches the heart sees through the pretense of not-knowing (cf. Ps 62:12; Rom 2:6).

13.text: Eat honey, my son, for it is good, and the honeycomb's drippings are sweet to your taste.
13.amp: My son [ben], eat [akal] honey [devash], for it is good [tov]; and the honeycomb [nopheth], which is sweet [matoq] to your taste [chek -- palate, the roof of the mouth].
13.notes: devash (H1706), honey, is the book's emblem of what is both pleasant and nourishing. The verse sets up the comparison of v.14: as honey is to the chek (H2441), the tasting palate, so wisdom is to the soul -- delightful and good at once, not a bitter medicine but a sweetness.

14.text: Know that wisdom is just such sweetness to your soul; if you find it, there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off.
14.amp: So know [yada] that wisdom [chokmah] is to your soul [nephesh]: when you have found [matsa] it, then there is [yesh] a reward [acharit -- a latter end, a future], and your hope [tikvah -- expectation, a cord stretched forward] shall not be cut off [karath].
14.notes: acharit (H319) is the 'latter end,' the outcome that waits down the road -- wisdom secures a future. tikvah (H8615) means hope but comes from a root for cord or thread (cf. Rahab's scarlet line, Josh 2); the wise man's lifeline to the future will not be karath (H3772), severed. Sweetness now (v.13) and a secured end -- both belong to wisdom.

15.text: Do not lie in ambush, you wicked man, against the home of the righteous; do not raid his place of rest.
15.amp: Do not lie in wait [arav -- ambush, crouch in hiding], O wicked [rasha] man, against the dwelling [naveh -- habitation, the resting fold of a flock] of the righteous [tsaddiq]; do not destroy [shadad -- ravage, lay waste] his resting place [revets -- his lair, his place of repose].
15.notes: arav (H693) is the predator's ambush; naveh (H5116) is a shepherd's settled fold, an image of peace and security. The warning is to the would-be raider: strike at the righteous and you strike at a man God Himself defends (v.16). Their security rests not on their walls but on the LORD.

16.text: For though a righteous man falls seven times, he rises again, but the wicked are brought down by calamity.
16.amp: For a just [tsaddiq] man falls [naphal] seven times [sheba -- seven, the number of fullness] and rises up again [qum -- stands, gets back up]; but the wicked [rasha] stumble [kashal -- totter and fall] into calamity [ra -- evil, ruin].
16.notes: the righteous and the wicked both fall -- the difference is rising. naphal (H5307) and qum (H6965) set the rhythm: down seven times (sheba, H7651, the full number, 'as often as it takes'), up again every time. The wicked, by contrast, fall once into ra (H7451) and do not get up. Resilience, not immunity, marks the righteous (cf. Mic 7:8).

17.text: Do not gloat when your enemy falls, and do not let your heart be glad when he stumbles,
17.amp: Do not rejoice [samach -- be glad, exult] when your enemy [oyev] falls [naphal], and do not let your heart [leb] be glad [gil -- spin with joy, exult] when he stumbles [kashal];
17.notes: two joy-verbs, samach (H8055) and gil (H1523), are forbidden here -- the same exuberant gladness that elsewhere belongs to harvest and worship is wrong when aimed at a fallen foe. To gloat over an enemy's ruin is to make oneself his judge, a seat the LORD will not share (v.18; cf. Job 31:29; Matt 5:44).

18.text: lest the LORD see it and it be evil in His eyes, and He turn His anger away from him.
18.amp: lest the LORD [YHWH] see [raah] it, and it be evil [raa] in His eyes [ayin], and He turn away [shub] His wrath [aph -- nostril, the flaring of anger] from him.
18.notes: aph (H639) literally means the nostril, anger pictured as the hot snorting of the nose. The sobering logic: God's wrath against your enemy may relent precisely because your gloating has become the greater offense. Vengeance belongs to the LORD, and He will not have it usurped (Rom 12:19).

19.text: Do not fret yourself over evildoers, and do not envy the wicked,
19.amp: Do not fret [charah -- to burn hot, to be inflamed with vexation] yourself because of evil [raa] men, neither be envious [qana -- jealous, consumed with longing] of the wicked [rasha];
19.notes: charah (H2734) is the inward burning of anger or agitation -- here, the resentful fretting that smolders when the wicked seem to prosper. Paired again with qana (H7065, the envy of v.1), it bookends the chapter's opening movement: the antidote to both is the certainty of v.20 (cf. Ps 37:1-2).

20.text: for the evil man has no future, and the lamp of the wicked will be snuffed out.
20.amp: for there shall be no reward [acharit -- latter end, future] to the evil [ra] man; the lamp [ner -- the household light] of the wicked [rasha] shall be put out [daak -- extinguished, quenched].
20.notes: the same acharit (H319) that wisdom secures for the righteous (v.14) is denied the wicked -- they have no 'latter end.' ner (H5216), the lamp, is the steady flame of a living, prospering household; its being snuffed out (daak, H1846) is the image of a line and a future extinguished (cf. 13:9; Job 18:5-6).

21.text: Fear the LORD, my son, and the king; do not take up with those bent on rebellion,
21.amp: My son [ben], fear [yare -- revere, stand in awe of] the LORD [YHWH] and the king [melek]; do not meddle [arab -- mix yourself in, throw in your lot] with those given to change [shanah -- the changers, the rebellious who would overturn order],
21.notes: yare (H3372), reverent fear, is owed first to the LORD and, under Him, to the king as His appointed order. arab (H6148) is to entangle oneself, to become surety with -- here, with the 'changers,' the restless rebels who agitate against legitimate authority. Their sudden ruin (v.22) is the reason to keep clear (cf. Rom 13:1-2; 1 Pet 2:17).

22.text: for disaster will rise against them suddenly, and who knows what ruin the two of them can bring?
22.amp: for their calamity [eyd -- disaster, the day of doom] shall rise [qum] suddenly [pithom -- in an instant, without warning]; and who knows [yada] the ruin [pid -- destruction, downfall] of them both [sheneyhem]?
22.notes: eyd (H343) is sudden catastrophe; pithom (H6597) underscores how fast it falls on the rebellious. 'Of them both' likely means the destruction that both the LORD and the king can unleash on rebels -- two powers the troublemaker has provoked at once, with consequences beyond his reckoning.

23.text: These also are sayings of the wise: to show partiality in judgment is not good.
23.amp: These things also belong to the wise [chakam]. To have respect [nakar -- to recognize a face, to favor] of persons [panim -- faces, presence] in judgment [mishpat -- justice, a legal verdict] is not good [tov].
23.notes: this verse heads a short appended collection ('further sayings of the wise'). The Hebrew idiom 'to recognize faces' (nakar panim, H5234 + H6440) means to let who a man is sway the verdict he gets -- the very corruption of mishpat (H4941). Justice is meant to be face-blind (cf. Lev 19:15; Deut 1:17).

24.text: Whoever says to the guilty, 'You are innocent,' will be cursed by peoples and denounced by nations;
24.amp: He who says [amar] to the wicked [rasha], 'You are righteous [tsaddiq],' him shall the peoples [am] curse [naqab -- denounce, pronounce a curse upon], nations [leom] shall abhor [zaam -- rage at, be indignant with] him;
24.notes: the corrupt judge who acquits the guilty (calls the rasha tsaddiq) earns public execration. naqab (H5344) is to pierce with a curse, to name in condemnation; zaam (H2194) is hot indignation. A whole society recoils, for a judge who reverses right and wrong tears the social fabric (cf. Isa 5:23).

25.text: but for those who convict the guilty there will be delight, and a rich blessing will come upon them.
25.amp: but to those who rebuke [yakach -- reprove, convict, set right] him shall be delight [naam -- be pleasant, go well], and a good [tov] blessing [berakah] shall come [bo] upon them.
25.notes: yakach (H3198) is to reprove and convict -- here the judge who rightly condemns the guilty rather than flattering them. The reward is the reverse of v.24's curse: not the nations' wrath but a 'blessing of good' (berakah, H1293) settling upon the upright judge. Right judgment is a public good that returns blessing on its doer.

26.text: An honest answer is like a kiss on the lips.
26.amp: He kisses [nashaq -- to kiss] the lips [saphah] who gives a right [nakoach -- straight, sincere, fitting] answer [dabar -- word, reply].
26.notes: the Hebrew is vivid: a straight, true answer (nakoach, H5228) is as welcome and intimate as a kiss on the lips (nashaq, H5401). Honest speech, even when it corrects, is an act of friendship; the truthful word is received with the warmth one gives a kiss (cf. 27:5-6).

27.text: Get your work ready outside and your fields in order; after that, build your house.
27.amp: Prepare [kun -- make ready, set in order] your work [melakah -- labor, occupation] outside [chuts -- in the open, the field], and make it fit [atad -- ready, prepared] for yourself in the field [sadeh]; and afterward [achar] build [banah] your house [bayith].
27.notes: kun (H3559), 'make ready,' echoes the establishing of v.3 -- but here as practical sequence: secure the means of livelihood (the field that feeds the family) before building the house and starting the household. First the productive labor, then the comforts; provision before settlement (cf. Luke 14:28-30).

28.text: Do not testify against your neighbor without cause, and do not deceive with your lips.
28.amp: Do not be a witness [ed -- one who testifies] against your neighbor [rea -- friend, fellow] without cause [chinnam -- gratuitously, for nothing], and do not deceive [pathah -- entice, mislead] with your lips [saphah].
28.notes: ed (H5707) is courtroom testimony; chinnam (H2600) means groundless, the same word for the harmless man attacked 'for no reason' in 1:11. To testify against a rea (H7453) without cause is false witness; pathah (H6601) warns that even true-sounding words can be a lure to deceive (cf. Exod 20:16).

29.text: Do not say, 'I will treat him as he treated me; I will pay the man back for what he did.'
29.amp: Do not say [amar], 'I will do [asah] to him as he has done [asah] to me; I will render [shub -- repay, return] to the man [ish] according to his deed [poal].'
29.notes: the verse forbids private retaliation -- repaying deed for deed (shub, H7725, 'render back'). The same repaying language used of God in v.12 is here denied to man: vengeance is the LORD's prerogative, not the wounded party's. To take it up is to seize a throne not yours (cf. 20:22; Rom 12:17-19).

30.text: I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard of a man with no sense,
30.amp: I went [abar -- passed over, crossed by] by the field [sadeh] of the slothful [atsel -- the sluggard, the lazy man], and by the vineyard [kerem] of the man [adam] lacking [chaser -- void of, missing] understanding [leb -- heart, here the seat of sense];
30.notes: the chapter ends with a parable from observation. atsel (H6102), the sluggard, is one of Proverbs' great cautionary figures (cf. 6:6-11). The man 'lacking heart' (chaser leb, H2638 + H3820) is void of sense -- in Hebrew thought the leb is the organ of judgment, so to lack it is to be a fool, not unfeeling but unthinking.

31.text: and there it was, all overgrown with thorns; the ground was buried under weeds, and its stone wall lay broken down.
31.amp: And, behold, it was all grown over [alah -- come up, spring up] with thorns [qimmoshon -- nettles, thistles], and nettles [charul -- weeds, briars] had covered [kasah -- concealed, blanketed] its surface [panim -- face], and its stone [even] wall [geder -- enclosing fence, boundary] was broken down [haras -- torn down, demolished].
31.notes: neglect, not catastrophe, did this: thorns came up (alah, H5927), weeds blanketed the face of the soil, and the protective geder (H1444) -- the stone wall that kept beasts out and the boundary in -- lay haras (H2040), torn down. Laziness does not merely fail to build; it lets what was built collapse into ruin.

32.text: I looked, and I took it to heart; I saw, and I learned a lesson:
32.amp: Then I saw [chazah -- to gaze, to behold, to perceive with insight] and set my heart [shith leb -- fixed my attention, laid it to heart] on it; I looked [raah] and received [laqach -- took, accepted] instruction [musar -- discipline, formative correction].
32.notes: the wise man does not just glance and move on -- chazah (H2372), to behold with discernment, and 'set the heart' (shith leb, H7896 + H3820) describe deliberate reflection. He takes (laqach, H3947) musar (H4148), the very corrective discipline named in the book's prologue (1:2), drawn here not from a teacher's words but from a ruined field. Wisdom learns from what it sees.

33.text: Just a bit more sleep, just a short doze, just a brief while with hands folded as I lie down --
33.amp: Yet a little [meat -- a small amount] sleep [shenah], a little [meat] slumber [tenumah -- drowsing, dozing], a little [meat] folding [chibbuq -- clasping, folding together] of the hands [yad] to lie down [shakab];
33.notes: the sluggard's self-talk, quoted nearly verbatim from 6:10. The thrice-repeated meat (H4592), 'just a little,' is the lie laziness tells itself -- each small indulgence sounds harmless. shakab (H7901) is to lie down; the folded hands (chibbuq, H2264) are the emblem of work refused.

34.text: and your poverty will come marching in like a vagrant, and your need like a man bearing arms.
34.amp: so shall your poverty [resh -- destitution, want] come [bo] like one who travels [halak -- walks, comes on the road] -- like a prowler -- and your want [machsor -- need, lack] like an armed [magen -- shield-bearing] man [ish].
34.notes: the consequence arrives unbidden and unstoppable: resh (H7389), poverty, walks in like a vagabond, and machsor (H4270), want, like a man with a shield (magen, H4043) -- a foe too strong to resist. The Hebrew idiom is 'a man of shield,' an armed raider. The sluggard who would not work cannot, in the end, fight off the ruin his idleness invited (cf. 6:11).
